content: Dry eye syndrome occurs when the eyes are unable to maintain a healthy layer of tears to coat their surface. Dry eye syndrome is commonly seen in individuals who are otherwise healthy. However, in rare cases, it can be associated with systemic autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus erythematosus, and other similar conditions. It may also result from thermal or chemical burns. In regions where malnutrition is prevalent, vitamin A deficiency can be a contributing factor, though this is rare in the United States. The risk of developing dry eye syndrome increases with age, as tear production naturally decreases over time. Signs of dry eye syndrome include reduced visual acuity and a thickened cornea. Diagnostic tests may involve a slit lamp (biomicroscope) examination of the tear film, often enhanced with a dye like fluorescein to make the tear film more visible. Another test, Schirmer's test, measures the rate of tear production using a calibrated paper strip placed on the edge of the eyelid. You should seek immediate medical attention if you experience dry eyes accompanied by a sudden increase in discomfort or redness, or if there is a sudden decrease in vision. Treatment options for dry eye syndrome include the use of hot compresses or eyelash cleaning, lubricating ointments for more severe cases, and medications such as cyclosporine (Restasis), topical corticosteroids, or oral antibiotics like tetracycline and doxycycline. Tiny plugs can be inserted into the tear drainage ducts to help retain tears on the eye's surface. Artificial tears, also known as wetting drops, are commonly used. In cases where the eyelids are abnormally positioned, surgery may be necessary. Most patients with dry eye syndrome experience discomfort but do not suffer from vision loss. However, in severe cases, the cornea—the clear window at the front of the eye—may become damaged or infected. Serious complications of dry eye syndrome include corneal ulcers or infections. There is no definitive way to prevent dry eye syndrome. However, complications can be minimized by using wetting and lubricating drops or ointments regularly.
